propositions.text: A man wearing a blue Halloween mask and holding a large knife robbed a variety store at night.
propositions.quote: A man wearing a blue Halloween mask and holding a large, butcher-style knife came into a variety store and demanded money from the woman working in the store that night.

propositions.text: The robber took money from the cash register and fled, actions caught on the store’s security camera.
propositions.quote: When she opened the cash register, the robber scooped money from the till and ran out of the store. His actions were caught by the store’s security camera.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a man in a blue Halloween mask robbed a store at night, taking money and fleeing, caught on security camera.

propositions.text: Police found a blue Halloween mask, a large knife, and a plastic cash register cover nearby the next morning.
propositions.quote: The next morning, police found a number of items in the neighbourhood: a blue Halloween mask, a large knife, and what turned out to be a plastic cover from the store’s cash register.

propositions.text: DNA on the blue mask matched only Marty David O’Brien with a probability of 1 in 33 billion.
propositions.quote: A test of the DNA found on the blue mask matched only one person: Marty David O’Brien. This match was characterized by the DNA expert in her report as follows: The estimated probability of selecting an unrelated individual at random from the Canadian Caucasian population . . . is 1 in 33 billion.

paragraphs.summary: The court states police found items including a blue mask with DNA matching only Marty David O’Brien, probability 1 in 33 billion.

propositions.text: Mr. O’Brien was charged and convicted of three offences, including robbery.
propositions.quote: Mr. O’Brien was charged and convicted of three offences, including robbery.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. O’Brien was charged and convicted of three offences including robbery.

propositions.text: At trial, nine witnesses testified before Justice Murphy without a jury.
propositions.quote: At a trial without a jury before Justice John D. Murphy, nine witnesses testified.

propositions.text: The investigating officer briefly referenced Mr. O’Brien’s prior criminal record and conduct during testimony.
propositions.quote: The investigating officer made brief references to Mr. O’Brien’s prior criminal record and conduct in the course of his testimony.

propositions.text: The defence did not object to this evidence nor request limiting it to narrative purpose.
propositions.quote: Not only was there no objection to this evidence by the defence nor any request that it be limited to a narrative purpose;

propositions.text: The defence used the prior record evidence in cross-examination of the investigating officer.
propositions.quote: the defence used the evidence in its cross-examination of the investigating officer: Okay. Now in your testimony you briefly stated that you knew Mr. O’Brien to be known as an offender and that’s why you sort of steered in his direction in terms of this particular incident.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports at trial, the investigating officer referenced O’Brien’s prior record; defence did not object and used it in cross-examination.

propositions.text: Only defence counsel referred to Mr. O’Brien’s reputation as a “known offender” in closing submissions.
propositions.quote: Only defence counsel, in closing submissions, referred again to Mr. O’Brien’s reputation as a “known offender”.

propositions.text: The Crown made no mention of character evidence in closing submissions and the trial judge made no reference to it.
propositions.quote: The Crown made no mention of the character evidence in its closing submission and the trial judge made no reference of any kind to it.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports only defence counsel mentioned O’Brien’s reputation in closing; Crown and judge did not mention character evidence.

propositions.text: Mr. O’Brien did not testify and the defence called no evidence.
propositions.quote: Mr. O’Brien did not testify and the defence called no evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. O’Brien did not testify and defence called no evidence.

propositions.text: Mr. O’Brien appealed to Nova Scotia Court of Appeal on ground that verdict was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The basis of Mr. O’Brien’s appeal to the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal was that the verdict was unreasonable.

propositions.text: Before hearing, court clerk asked counsel to address character evidence though it was not raised in appeal notice or factum.
propositions.quote: Before the hearing, the clerk of the court, at the panel’s request, wrote to counsel and asked that they be prepared to address the issue of character evidence. Mr. O’Brien had not raised this issue as a ground of appeal either in his notice of appeal or his factum.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports O’Brien appealed on unreasonableness; court asked counsel to address character evidence not raised in appeal documents.

propositions.text: The Crown acknowledged trial judge erred by not excluding or qualifying character evidence but argued it was not serious error.
propositions.quote: At the appeal, the Crown acknowledged that it was an error for the trial judge not to exclude the character evidence or qualify its purpose, but submitted that since it was not a serious error, the curative proviso in s. 686(1) (b)(iii) of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 , should be applied.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown acknowledges trial judge erred on character evidence but argues error was not serious and curative proviso applies.

propositions.text: All three judges found verdict not unreasonable but majority held trial judge erred seriously by allowing character evidence.
propositions.quote: All three judges concluded that the verdict was not unreasonable. The majority held, however, that the trial judge made a serious error in allowing the character evidence to be heard.

propositions.text: Majority found no indication trial judge disabused himself of character evidence or knew it could not be considered.
propositions.quote: there was no indication that he “disabused himself from that evidence or was otherwise aware that it could not be considered” (2010 NSCA 61, 293 N.S.R. (2d) 78, at para. 94).

propositions.text: Crown did not discharge burden to show judge was not influenced consciously or unconsciously by prejudicial evidence.
propositions.quote: The Crown had, as a result, not discharged its onus of demonstrating that the judge was not influenced, “consciously or unconsciously”, by the impugned prejudicial evidence (para. 95).

propositions.text: Curative proviso was unavailable; appeal allowed and new trial ordered.
propositions.quote: The curative proviso was therefore not available. The appeal was allowed and a new trial ordered.

paragraphs.summary: The majority of the Court of Appeal found serious error in admitting character evidence, no proof judge was uninfluenced, and ordered new trial.

propositions.text: Dissenting judge would have dismissed appeal, finding error was not serious and caused no miscarriage of justice.
propositions.quote: The dissenting judge, Fichaud J.A., would have dismissed the appeal. In his view, the error in hearing the investigating officer’s propensity evidence was not a serious one and caused no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

propositions.text: Dissent found trial judge’s reasons affirmatively show improper evidence had no impact and relied entirely on DNA evidence.
propositions.quote: The trial judge’s written reasons satisfy me affirmatively that the improper evidence had no impact. This, in my view, satisfies the Crown’s burden under the proviso. The judge’s words that he relied “entirely on the DNA evidence” to connect Mr. O’Brien to the robbery exclude any imputation to the judge of a veiled line of reasoning sourced in [the investigating officer’s] problematic testimony.

propositions.text: Dissent disagreed with majority’s view that judge’s reliance on DNA excludes improper evidence influence.
propositions.quote: My colleague does not explain how such a veiled line of reasoning can co-exist with the judge’s clear statement that he relied “entirely on the DNA evidence.”

propositions.text: Dissent concluded curative proviso was available and shared this view.
propositions.quote: The curative proviso was therefore available. I share this view.

paragraphs.summary: The dissenting judge found the error harmless, trial judge relied entirely on DNA, and curative proviso applied, so would dismiss appeal.

propositions.text: Whether trial judge’s error admitting bad character evidence and failure to address it was harmless or outside curative proviso.
propositions.quote: The issue before us was whether the trial judge’s error in hearing “bad character” evidence — and his related failure to specifically address that evidence in his reasons — was a harmless one, or whether it was outside the borders of the curative proviso.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is whether the trial judge’s error admitting bad character evidence was harmless or outside the curative proviso.

propositions.text: At trial, identification was the only issue; trial judge cautioned himself to approach such evidence with care.
propositions.quote: At trial, the only issue was identification. The trial judge cautioned himself about the need to approach such evidence with care, then concluded (2009 NSSC 194, 279 N.S.R. (2d) 157, at paras. 6-7):

propositions.text: Trial judge found strong circumstantial evidence linking blue mask to robbery beyond reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: We then have the circumstantial evidence of a blue mask being found the following morning a short distance from the store, on a route which leads toward the car. We also have the knife and the cash register part found the following day close to the blue mask. I am satisfied that the circumstantial evidence is strong and sufficient to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that there is a connection between the blue mask and the robbery of the convenience store . . . on the previous evening.

propositions.text: Video showed someone wearing blue mask and knife; cash register part linked to store by employee’s notations.
propositions.quote: Given the fact that the video clearly shows someone wearing a blue mask, or the blue and black mask, it clearly shows the use of a knife, and the evidence from the person who was in charge of the cash at the store, who returned to the store that night, clearly links the cash register part found to the cash register, because her notations and notations of others were on it.

propositions.text: Trial judge was satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that blue mask was associated with the robbery.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the evidence establishes that the blue mask was associated with the robbery, and I am convinced of that beyond a reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Investigating officer’s character evidence played no role in this finding.
propositions.quote: The investigating officer’s character evidence played no role in this finding.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found strong circumstantial evidence linking the blue mask to the robbery and that character evidence played no role.

propositions.text: Trial judge stated the question was whether the mask was connected to Mr. O’Brien beyond reasonable doubt, depending entirely on DNA evidence.
propositions.quote: The question then becomes whether the mask is connected to the accused, to Mr. O’Brien beyond a reasonable doubt, and that depends, as I have indicated, entirely on the DNA evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge stated the identification depended entirely on DNA evidence connecting the mask to Mr. O’Brien.

propositions.text: Trial judge concluded DNA evidence clearly ties Mr. O’Brien to the mask based on irrefutable match.
propositions.quote: After reviewing the DNA evidence for several paragraphs, the trial judge concluded that it “clearly ties” Mr. O’Brien to the mask, based on the irrefutable match between his DNA and the DNA found in the mask (para. 13).

propositions.text: Trial judge concluded DNA evidence establishes accused’s identity as robber beyond reasonable doubt, tying him to the blue mask.
propositions.quote: . . . the DNA evidence establishes the accused’s identity as the robber beyond a reasonable doubt, ties him to the blue mask which was found, which I have indicated, based on circumstantial evidence, is clearly the mask that was used in the robbery.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge concluded DNA evidence irrefutably ties Mr. O’Brien to the mask and establishes his identity as the robber beyond reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Propensity evidence from investigating officer played no part in convictions; trial judge relied entirely on DNA evidence.
propositions.quote: The propensity evidence from the investigating officer clearly played no part in the convictions. As Fichaud J.A. noted, not only did the trial judge expressly state that he relied entirely on the DNA evidence to identify Mr. O’Brien, his detailed reasons confirm this exclusive reliance.

propositions.text: When trial judge expressly concludes independently of inadmissible evidence, no unfairness or miscarriage of justice arises (R. v. Leaney, R. v. Khan).
propositions.quote: This evokes the words of McLachlin J. in R. v. Leaney, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 393, at pp. 415-16, where she noted that when a trial judge expressly arrives at a conclusion on the critical issue “independently of the inadmissible evidence . . . no unfairness can be said to arise, nor has there been a miscarriage of justice” (see also R. v. Khan, 2001 SCC 86, [2001] 3 S.C.R. 823, at para. 30).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the propensity evidence played no part; trial judge relied entirely on DNA, consistent with precedent on inadmissible evidence.

propositions.text: Trial judge’s statement of relying entirely on DNA means he did not rely on character evidence.
propositions.quote: The trial judge said in his reasons that he relied “entirely” on the DNA evidence (para. 8). That meant that he did not rely on the character evidence.

propositions.text: Imputing reliance on character evidence despite contrary reasons creates uncharted appellate review where silence is seen as unconscious error.
propositions.quote: Imputing such reliance into reasons that state the contrary creates a new, unchartable universe of appellate review where even if the reasons reveal a proper grasp of the facts and the law, the trial judge may nonetheless find the integrity of his or her decision undermined by the possibility that judicial silence on an issue will be interpreted as “unconscious” judicial error.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge did not rely on character evidence and imputing otherwise creates problematic appellate review.

propositions.text: Trial judges must show how result was reached but need not itemize every issue or thought process.
propositions.quote: A trial judge has an obligation to demonstrate through his or her reasons how the result was arrived at. This does not create a requirement to itemize every conceivable issue, argument or thought process.

propositions.text: Trial judges’ reasons are reviewed based on what they say, not speculative imagination; perfection is not required (R. v. Sheppard).
propositions.quote: Trial judges are entitled to have their reasons reviewed based on what they say, not on the speculative imagination of reviewing courts. As Binnie J. noted in R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 869, at para. 55, trial judges should not be held to some “abstract standard of perfection”.

paragraphs.summary: The court states trial judges must explain results but not every thought; reasons are reviewed as written, not speculatively, and perfection is not required.

propositions.text: Trial judge’s reasoning was impeccable and shows no subconscious subversion of articulated thoughts.
propositions.quote: The trial judge was entitled to be taken at his word. His chain of fact, law and logic in this case was impeccable. I see nothing about his approach that suggests a subconscious subversion of his articulated thoughts.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge’s reasoning impeccable with no subconscious error.

propositions.text: The admission of improper character evidence was a harmless error causing no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.
propositions.quote: I therefore agree with Fichaud J.A. that the admission of the improper character evidence was a harmless error of law that caused no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the improper character evidence admission was a harmless error causing no miscarriage of justice.

propositions.text: The court would allow the appeal and restore the convictions.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal and restore the convictions.

paragraphs.summary: The court would allow the appeal and restore convictions.

propositions.text: The Crown relies on DNA evidence to uphold convictions from an unfair trial.
propositions.quote: the Crown invokes the magic of DNA evidence to salvage convictions obtained in what all the judges of the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal agreed was an unfair trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Crown relies on DNA evidence to uphold convictions from an unfair trial.

propositions.text: The respondent was convicted as the masked robber with identification as the only live issue.
propositions.quote: The respondent was convicted as the “masked robber” of a convenience store in Amherst, Nova Scotia. The only live issue was identification.

propositions.text: No evidence linked the respondent to the crime except DNA on masks found near the scene.
propositions.quote: There was no evidence, circumstantial or otherwise, linking him to the crime except for traces of DNA on one of two masks later found abandoned near the scene of the crime.

propositions.text: Unfairness arose because police told the court about the respondent's unrelated criminal reputation.
propositions.quote: The unfairness arose because the police, in the absence of such other evidence, decided to tell the court all about the respondent’s reputation as a habitual criminal in relation to other matters unconnected to the offences for which he was charged.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the respondent was convicted as the masked robber based only on DNA, with unfairness from police revealing unrelated criminal reputation.

propositions.text: The trial judge admitted propensity evidence without comment and failed to recognize its unfairness.
propositions.quote: The trial judge let in the propensity evidence without comment and gave no hint in his reasons that he recognized that the police branding of the respondent as a career criminal was against basic principles of trial fairness.

propositions.text: Trial judges may misapply the law, necessitating appellate review.
propositions.quote: Trial judges may be presumed to know the law but occasionally they misapply it. Otherwise, there would be no need for appellate courts.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge admitted propensity evidence unfairly and notes appellate courts are needed for such misapplications.

propositions.text: The respondent, sentenced to over six years, deserves assurance the trial judge recognized propensity evidence dangers.
propositions.quote: The respondent, now sentenced to six years and six months in prison, is entitled to know that the trial judge recognized the danger of propensity evidence and consciously put it aside.

propositions.text: The trial judge’s reasons provide no assurance he recognized the danger of propensity evidence.
propositions.quote: The trial judge’s reasons provide no assurance on that point (2009 NSSC 194, 279 N.S.R. (2d) 157).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the respondent deserves assurance the trial judge recognized propensity evidence dangers, but the judge’s reasons provide no such assurance.

propositions.text: A majority finds the trial judge’s use of 'entirely' renders unfairness harmless, but the court disagrees.
propositions.quote: A majority of my colleagues conclude that the trial judge’s use of the word “entirely” in relation to his reliance on the DNA evidence is enough to render the unfairness of the trial harmless.

propositions.text: Relying on 'entirely' ignores trial context and DNA evidence handling problems causing wrongful convictions.
propositions.quote: To do so, in my view, ignores the context of the trial as a whole. The reliability of DNA science is well established, but problems in the handling of DNA samples and management of the test results have given rise to a number of wrongful convictions where (as here) there was not a shred of other probative evidence to connect an accused to the crime.

propositions.text: The curative proviso requires the Crown to prove no substantial wrong or miscarriage despite unfair trial.
propositions.quote: The curative proviso in s. 686(1) (b)(iii) of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 , requires the Crown, not the defence, to show that despite the unfair trial, there was no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

propositions.text: The court does not believe the Crown discharged its onus and would dismiss the appeal.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I do not believe that the Crown has discharged its onus. I agree with the caution exercised by the majority in the court below. I would dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with the majority that 'entirely' renders unfairness harmless, holds the Crown must prove no miscarriage, and would dismiss the appeal.

propositions.text: The Crown sought to portray the respondent as a bad person likely to commit the robbery.
propositions.quote: The Crown’s evidence at trial sought to portray the respondent as a “bad person” of the sort likely to commit the robbery of a convenience store.

propositions.text: Beveridge J.A. found the inadmissible evidence was extensive and showed the accused was known to police for similar offences.
propositions.quote: Beveridge J.A. stated that “the inadmissible evidence was no mere inadvertent slip. It went on for some pages in the transcript. It included evidence that the [accused] was known to the police to be involved in the very type of offence before the court” (2010 NSCA 61, 293 N.S.R. (2d) 78, at para. 68).

propositions.text: The Crown cannot prove its case by showing accused's misconduct unrelated to the charged offence.
propositions.quote: It has been established for over 100 years that the Crown cannot make its case by showing that the accused engaged in misconduct other than that alleged against him for the purpose of showing that the accused was the type of person who would commit the crime alleged.

propositions.text: Police investigator testified the respondent was thought involved in multiple incidents and was known as an active criminal in the area.
propositions.quote: So just at this particular time in 2004 in October there was . . . Marty O’Brien was thought to be involved in a number of incidences [sic] within Amherst and within the county . . . .

propositions.text: The officer testified the respondent was known within the RCMP as an active criminal in the area.
propositions.quote: I’ve known Marty O’Brien and he’s known me for years. I don’t know, maybe 10 or maybe 15, 20 years, and I know his . . . I don’t know everything he does, but I know his criminal background, and it was common knowledge within our office and within the RCMP detachment in Amherst that Marty O’Brien was an active criminal who was traveling Amherst . . . Cumberland County area, and we were aware that Marty was involved in these activities.

propositions.text: The policeman spoke to the respondent who denied involvement; later DNA order was issued and monitored.
propositions.quote: So I went to the county jail, and I spoke to Marty O’Brien with regards to his being involved and he denied any involvement in it whatsoever. So I . . . after this, I checked . . . later on it became known that Marty O’Brien was convicted in court for a number of offences and a DNA order was issued to be taken on Marty O’Brien. So I continued to monitor DNA orders.

propositions.text: This general evidence of criminality was unrelated to the charged offences.
propositions.quote: This general “evidence” of criminality was unrelated to the offences as charged.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports the Crown portrayed the respondent as a bad person, inadmissible evidence was extensive, police testified to his criminal reputation unrelated to the charges.

propositions.text: Defence counsel did not object and the trial judge did not intervene or express concern about the evidence.
propositions.quote: It is true that counsel for the defence did not object. Nor did the trial judge intervene or otherwise express any concern about (or even awareness of) the impropriety of the evidence.

propositions.text: Both majority and minority in the court below found the bad character evidence wholly inadmissible and the trial unfair.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, both the majority and the minority in the court below found the evidence of bad character to be wholly inadmissible and the trial on that account to be unfair.

propositions.text: Prejudice in this context is the risk of an unfocused trial and wrongful conviction, not just risk of conviction.
propositions.quote: It is frequently mentioned that “prejudice” in this context is not the risk of conviction. It is, more properly, the risk of an unfocussed trial and a wrongful conviction.

propositions.text: Forbidden reasoning infers guilt from general disposition or propensity, undermining presumption of innocence.
propositions.quote: The forbidden chain of reasoning is to infer guilt from general disposition or propensity. The evidence, if believed, shows that an accused has discreditable tendencies. In the end, the verdict may be based on prejudice rather than proof, thereby undermining the presumption of innocence enshrined in ss. 7 and 11 (d) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms .

propositions.text: Propensity evidence predisposes the trier of fact to accept guilt more readily than warranted.
propositions.quote: Propensity evidence is designed to predispose the trier of fact to accept more readily as credible the guilt of the accused than would otherwise be the case.

propositions.text: Beveridge J.A. noted the use of propensity evidence was not a mere inadvertent slip.
propositions.quote: As mentioned, Beveridge J.A. noted that its use in this case “was no mere inadvertent slip” (para. 68).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes defence did not object, trial judge did not intervene, and the court below found the bad character evidence inadmissible and trial unfair due to propensity evidence risks.

propositions.text: Identification of the respondent as perpetrator rested on two strands: the red car and DNA evidence.
propositions.quote: The identification of the respondent as the perpetrator rested on two strands of evidence. (1) The Red Car

paragraphs.summary: The court states identification rested on two strands: red car and DNA evidence.

propositions.text: A red car was seen near the mask location; respondent’s ex-girlfriend owned a red car he had access to.
propositions.quote: At about the same time as the robbery, a red car was seen by a witness leaving the general area where the mask and other items were subsequently found. The respondent’s former girlfriend testified that she owned a red car to which, during the relationship, the respondent had “access”.

propositions.text: The ex-girlfriend did not confirm the relationship was ongoing or identify the car seen as hers.
propositions.quote: She did not say the relationship was continuing as of the date of the robbery or that he had continuing access. The witness was shown pictures of the former girlfriend’s car, but did not identify this car as the one she saw, or provide any identifying features about it except that the car she saw was red.

propositions.text: The trial judge correctly concluded the red car evidence was essentially unhelpful.
propositions.quote: The trial judge correctly concluded that the “red car” evidence was essentially unhelpful.

propositions.text: The second strand of identification evidence was DNA evidence.
propositions.quote: (2) The DNA Evidence

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the red car evidence as unhelpful and notes DNA evidence as the second identification strand.

propositions.text: DNA from two masks was recovered; one matched the respondent’s DNA.
propositions.quote: A forensic expert recovered DNA from the two abandoned face masks and testified that in the case of one of the masks, the DNA matched that of the respondent.

propositions.text: DNA evidence alone does not prove guilt of the offence.
propositions.quote: Evidence of a “match” does not, of course, prove guilt of the offence.

propositions.text: The Crown acknowledged DNA evidence only shows contact with the mask, not that the respondent was the masked robber.
propositions.quote: The Crown acknowledged that the DNA evidence in this case was the equivalent to that of a fingerprint in the sense that it established that at some point in time the respondent had handled or even worn the mask. It did not, without more, establish that the respondent was the masked robber on October 11, 2004.

paragraphs.summary: The court states DNA matched the respondent but does not prove guilt; the Crown acknowledged it only shows contact with the mask.

propositions.text: The trial judge relied entirely on DNA evidence to link the respondent to the mask used in the robbery.
propositions.quote: The trial judge said that he relied “entirely” on the DNA evidence to link the respondent to the mask, which the trial judge concluded (on other evidence) was the mask used in the robbery.

propositions.text: An inferential leap is required from DNA contact to finding the respondent wore the mask to commit the robbery.
propositions.quote: However, an inferential leap must still be made from a finding that the respondent once came into contact with the mask to a finding that he actually donned the mask to commit the robbery.

propositions.text: DNA evidence alone does little to bridge the gap unless combined with knowledge of the respondent as a career criminal implicated in similar incidents.
propositions.quote: DNA evidence alone does little to bridge this analytical gap — unless one was also given the information from Sgt. Blakeney that it is not just any random member of the community whose DNA has been found on the mask, but the DNA of a career criminal who was known to be implicated in a string of similar incidents in the same area around the same time.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge relied entirely on DNA evidence, but an inferential leap is needed to link the respondent to the robbery without the bad character evidence.

propositions.text: Section 686(1)(b)(iii) allows upholding a conviction despite trial judge's legal error if no substantial wrong or miscarriage occurred.
propositions.quote: Section 686(1) (b)(iii) permits an appellate court to uphold a conviction despite error of law committed by the trial judge where that error has not led to a substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

propositions.text: The legal error was admitting evidence portraying the respondent as a career criminal likely to commit the robbery.
propositions.quote: The error of law in this case was the admission of the evidence portraying the respondent as a career criminal — exactly the sort of person one might expect robbed this convenience store.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the legal error was admitting bad character evidence, and the curative proviso allows upholding conviction if no miscarriage occurred.

propositions.text: The curative proviso applies only if the trial outcome would necessarily be the same despite the error.
propositions.quote: The “curative proviso” is to be applied only in those cases where the outcome of the trial, irrespective of the error, would necessarily have been the same (Colpitts v. The Queen, [1965] S.C.R. 739).

propositions.text: The Crown bears the onus to establish the high standard for applying the curative proviso.
propositions.quote: The onus of establishing that this high standard is met is on the Crown: R. v. Jolivet, 2000 SCC 29, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 751; R. v. Khan, 2001 SCC 86, [2001] 3 S.C.R. 823; R. v. Van, 2009 SCC 22, [2009] 1 S.C.R. 716.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the curative proviso applies only if the trial outcome would be the same despite error, and the Crown bears the onus to prove this.

propositions.text: The curative proviso applies if Crown proves on balance of probabilities that error was harmless or evidence overwhelming.
propositions.quote: The curative proviso may be applied, according to its modern interpretation, where the Crown can establish on a balance of probabilities that the legal error is harmless, in the sense that no prejudice has resulted, or that, despite any prejudice caused by the trial judge’s error of law, the evidence against the accused is so overwhelming that a trier of fact would inevitably convict: Khan, at paras. 26-31; Jolivet, at paras. 48-54; Van, at paras. 34-36.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the curative proviso applies if the Crown proves the error was harmless or evidence overwhelming on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Relying on the trial judge’s silence or use of 'entirely' is insufficient to apply the curative proviso.
propositions.quote: In the application of the curative proviso on the facts of this case, I do not think that it is sufficient to rely on the trial judge’s silence on the issues of the inadmissible police evidence. Nor should the Court’s refusal of a new trial hang on the thread of the trial judge’s use of the word “entirely” which — it seems to me — just reflects the fact that there was no other identification evidence before him.

propositions.text: If the trial judge intended to distance himself from the inadmissible evidence, he would have said so.
propositions.quote: If he had intended by the word “entirely” to distance himself from the inadmissible propensity evidence, I expect he would have said so.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge’s silence and use of 'entirely' do not suffice to apply the curative proviso or show distancing from inadmissible evidence.

propositions.text: The court’s concern does not impute flawed reasoning based on speculation but reflects the Crown’s burden to prove harmlessness.
propositions.quote: My concern does not “impute” flawed reasoning to the trial judge on the basis of “speculative imagination” (reasons of Abella J., at paras. 16-17). Rather, it reflects the general principle that the Crown, not the defence, bears the burden of showing that the improper evidence was “harmless”.

propositions.text: Abella J.’s reasoning reverses the Crown’s burden of proof.
propositions.quote: In my respectful view, Abella J.’s reasoning is tantamount to reversing the Crown’s burden of proof.

paragraphs.summary: The court states its concern reflects the Crown’s burden to prove harmlessness and criticizes Abella J. for reversing that burden.

propositions.text: The respondent argues bad character evidence prejudiced the trial judge to accept DNA evidence uncritically.
propositions.quote: The respondent argues that the evidence of bad character was prejudicial because it predisposed the trial judge to uncritical acceptance of the DNA evidence.

propositions.text: The respondent submits DNA evidence impact could be dangerously exaggerated by knowledge of his proclivities.
propositions.quote: The submission on his behalf was that “[t]he impact of DNA evidence found on the Halloween mask could have been dangerously inadvertently exaggerated by the judicial knowledge of Mr. O’Brien’s ‘proclivities’” (R.F., at para. 28).

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues bad character evidence prejudiced the trial judge to accept DNA evidence uncritically and exaggerated its impact.

propositions.text: The Crown says the trial judge was unaffected by bad character evidence because he did not mention it in reasons.
propositions.quote: The Crown’s response is that the trial judge was not affected by the evidence of bad character because he didn’t mention it in his reasons.

propositions.text: Beveridge J.A. noted the trial judge gave no indication of awareness of the problem during evidence or in reasons.
propositions.quote: However, as noted by Beveridge J.A., the trial judge gave no indication that he was even aware of the problem — either when the evidence was being adduced or in his reasons for judgment.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues the trial judge was unaffected by bad character evidence, but Beveridge J.A. found no indication the judge was aware of the problem.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal majority declined the curative proviso partly because no other evidence linked the respondent to the crime.
propositions.quote: In this case, the majority in the Court of Appeal declined to apply the curative proviso in part because there was no other evidence linking the respondent to the crime.

propositions.text: Fingerprint evidence connects a person to an object but linking to the crime requires other evidence of touching at relevant time and place.
propositions.quote: Fingerprint evidence will almost always afford cogent evidence that the person whose fingerprint is left on the object touched that object. However, the ability of the fingerprint evidence to connect an accused to the crime charged will depend on whether there is other evidence capable of establishing that the accused touched the object at the relevant time and place so as to connect the accused to the crime.

propositions.text: Mars was distinguished in Samuels where other evidence linked accused to the crime.
propositions.quote: In R. v. Samuels, 2009 ONCA 719 (CanLII), by contrast, Mars was distinguished on the basis that there was “other evidence” linking the accused to the crime (para. 17).

paragraphs.summary: The court reports the Court of Appeal majority declined the curative proviso due to lack of other evidence linking the respondent, citing Mars and Samuels.

propositions.text: The Crown concedes DNA on the mask alone does not establish the accused’s culpability.
propositions.quote: The Crown here concedes that the fact DNA was found on the blue/black mask does not, on its own, establish the . . . culpability [of the accused]

propositions.text: DNA presence is equivalent to a fingerprint; small amounts can be present for years and can be transferred by handling.
propositions.quote: The presence of the appellant’s DNA on the mask is equivalent to a fingerprint. The Crown’s expert testified that only small amounts of DNA are sufficient, and can be present for years. In addition, the thrust of the Crown’s expert evidence was that DNA can be transferred or deposited by handling.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports the Crown concedes DNA alone does not establish culpability and DNA can be transferred or persist for years.

propositions.text: I do not agree with Abella J. that admission of evidence blackening respondent's character was harmless.
propositions.quote: I do not agree with Abella J. that admission of the evidence blackening the character of the respondent was harmless.

propositions.text: Trial judge's failure to address problematic police evidence is a serious deficiency.
propositions.quote: The failure of the trial judge’s reasons to address the problematic police evidence is a deficiency that cannot simply be brushed off by reference to his use of the word “entirely”.

propositions.text: The Crown argues trial judges are presumed to know the law.
propositions.quote: The Crown argues that trial judges are presumed to know the law.

propositions.text: Argument excusing trial reason deficiencies by presuming judges know law was rejected in R. v. Sheppard and should be rejected here.
propositions.quote: the argument that important deficiencies in trial reasons can be excused on the basis that trial judges are presumed to know the law was rejected as a general one-size-fits-all excuse in R. v. Sheppard, 2002 SCC 26, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 869, and should be rejected here as well.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with Abella J. that harmful evidence admission was harmless, finds trial judge's failure serious, rejects Crown's presumption argument citing Sheppard.

propositions.text: The Crown invokes R. v. Leaney where inadmissible police opinion evidence was deemed surplusage and curative proviso applied.
propositions.quote: The Crown invokes R. v. Leaney, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 393. In that case, inadmissible opinion evidence was received from police officers but the curative proviso was nevertheless applied, per McLachlin J., at p. 415: Given the trial judge’s clear statement that he arrived at his conclusion as to identify independently of the evidence of the police officers, their evidence assumes the character of mere surplusage, which does not vitiate the judge’s conclusion that Leaney was one of persons shown on the video screen.

propositions.text: There is a significant difference between Leaney's inadmissible opinion evidence and prejudicial bad character evidence here.
propositions.quote: there is a significant difference between appellate tolerance of inadmissible opinion evidence in circumstances where the trial judge found that the opinion evidence was unnecessary to enable him to appreciate what he could see with his own eyes on a video (and the inadmissible opinions thus characterized as “mere surplusage”) and prejudicial evidence of bad character.

propositions.text: In Leaney, the officers' testimony content was unobjectionable; here, the information itself is objectionable.
propositions.quote: The content of the officers’ testimony in Leaney was itself unobjectionable. The problem was that it was not their place to utter it. Here, in contrast, it is the information itself, and not just its source, that is objectionable.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown cites Leaney where inadmissible police opinion was surplusage; the court finds bad character evidence here is fundamentally different and objectionable.

propositions.text: The Crown should not benefit from the curative proviso because trial judge showed no awareness of police testimony problem.
propositions.quote: the Crown should not have the benefit of the curative proviso because the trial judge’s reasons demonstrated no awareness of the problem of the police testimony.

propositions.text: In R. v. Rahm, no miscarriage of justice found where trial judge understood bad character was inadmissible if not in issue.
propositions.quote: This was not a jury case. During the course of the trial, the trial judge made it clear that he understood that bad character was not admissible where character had not been placed in issue.

propositions.text: No such understanding is evident in this trial judge's reasons.
propositions.quote: No such understanding is evident in the trial reasons in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no curative proviso benefit as trial judge showed no awareness of police testimony problem unlike Rahm case.

propositions.text: Trial judge's error of law cannot be dismissed as harmless; respondent is entitled to a new trial unless harmlessness is affirmatively found.
propositions.quote: I do not believe that the trial judge’s error of law can be dismissed as “harmless”, and, unless we can make an affirmative finding to that effect, the respondent is entitled to a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the trial judge's error is not harmless and respondent deserves a new trial absent affirmative harmlessness finding.

propositions.text: Curative proviso may apply if error is not harmless but evidence of guilt is overwhelming making guilty verdict inevitable.
propositions.quote: The curative proviso may also be applied when, despite an error of law that is not harmless, the case against an accused is so overwhelming that a guilty verdict would be the only reasonable outcome of a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court states curative proviso applies if error is not harmless but guilt evidence is overwhelming.

propositions.text: In Court of Appeal, Crown did not argue case was so strong that conviction was inevitable; dissenting judge agreed.
propositions.quote: In the Court of Appeal, the Crown did not even argue that its case was so strong that a trier of fact would inevitably convict. Nor did the dissenting judge make any such suggestion.

propositions.text: These concessions by Crown and dissenting judge were correct.
propositions.quote: In my view, these concessions were correct.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Crown and dissenting judge conceded case was not inevitably convicting, and agrees with them.

propositions.text: It is exceptional to deny new trial based on appellate conjecture of harmless error or overwhelming evidence.
propositions.quote: It is an exceptional thing to deny an accused the new trial to which he is otherwise entitled because of an appellate court’s conjecture that the error was “harmless” or that any reasonable trier of fact, properly instructed, would simply find the evidence of guilt to be overwhelming.

paragraphs.summary: The court states denying a new trial based on appellate conjecture of harmless error or overwhelming evidence is exceptional.

propositions.text: In R. v. Trochym, burden on Crown to invoke curative proviso is higher than proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: the burden on the Crown seeking to invoke the curative proviso “is a substantially higher one than the requirement that the Crown prove its case ‘beyond a reasonable doubt’ at trial”.

propositions.text: Appellate standard requires evidence be so overwhelming that conviction is inevitable, reflecting difficulty of retroactive effect assessment.
propositions.quote: The standard applied by an appellate court, namely that the evidence against an accused is so overwhelming that conviction is inevitable or would invariably result, is a substantially higher one than the requirement that the Crown prove its case “beyond a reasonable doubt” at trial. This higher standard reflects the fact that it is difficult for an appellate court . . . to consider retroactively the effect that, for example, excluding certain evidence could reasonably have had on the outcome.

propositions.text: The Crown cannot establish its case against respondent was overwhelming.
propositions.quote: In my view, the Crown cannot establish that its case against the respondent was “overwhelming”.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Trochym that Crown's burden for curative proviso is higher than beyond reasonable doubt and finds Crown's case not overwhelming.

propositions.text: I agree with majority below that curative proviso does not apply and would dismiss the appeal.
propositions.quote: I agree with the majority opinion in the court below that the curative proviso has no application, and accordingly I would dismiss the appeal.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed with Binnie and LeBel JJ. dissenting.
propositions.quote: Appeal allowed, Binnie and LeBel JJ. dissenting.

propositions.text: Solicitor for appellant is Public Prosecution Service of Nova Scotia, Halifax.
propositions.quote: Solicitor for the appellant: Public Prosecution Service of Nova Scotia, Halifax.

propositions.text: Solicitor for respondent is Nova Scotia Legal Aid, Amherst.
propositions.quote: Solicitor for the respondent: Nova Scotia Legal Aid, Amherst.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with majority below that curative proviso does not apply and dismisses appeal; notes solicitors and dissent.
